e-9829.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Diagonal Matrix
e-9829.problem:
For the matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095495/assets/d19df62851eeb549464dd522cabcb4f5ab982ed4cdf39a81e6c18642299270f2.png) find the pseudoinverse $A^+.$
e-9829.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m \times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
\sigma_1, \: \sigma_2, \: \ldots, \: \sigma_r
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n \times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma_1^{-1}}, \, {\sigma_2^{-1}}, \, \ldots, \, {\sigma_r^{-1}}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{6}^{-1} & \,\,\,0 & 0 \\ \,\,0 & \,{4}^{-1} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

e-9828.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Singular Value Decomposition
e-9828.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095495/assets/1727ec75ec656a46caa6228d4b4704643039a194cc2c33419ec8049f63a96a9c.png)
Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse $A^+.$
e-9828.worked_solution:
If $A=U \Sigma V ^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V \, \Sigma^+ \, U^T,
$$

where $\Sigma^+$ is the pseudoinverse of $\Sigma.$ 

First, notice that

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095495/assets/877912dffd62a0657f08fc4bc28158e1199daadbda3d92610a0c0f63055f5960.png)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0 \\ -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0 \\ -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0 \\ -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{4}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {3}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

For an "almost" zero m×n matrix with non-zero entries

σ1,σ2,…,σr

σ1−1,σ2−1,…,σr−1

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Diagonal Matrix
content.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{4}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {3}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{3}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

For an "almost" zero m×n matrix with non-zero entries

σ1,σ2,…,σr

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero n×m matrix with entries

σ1−1,σ2−1,…,σr−1

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain

A+=[3000]+=[3−1000]=13[1000].

verification.explanation: The revealed worked solution declares option c: reciprocate the nonzero diagonal entry 3 and leave the zero unchanged. This agrees with the independent calculation A⁺ = diag(1/3, 0).

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Diagonal Matrix
content.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{3}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{6}^{-1} & \,\,\,0 & 0 \\ \,\,0 & \,(-9)^{-1} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{18}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

For an "almost" zero m×n matrix with non-zero entries

σ1,σ2,…,σr

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero n×m matrix with entries

σ1−1,σ2−1,…,σr−1

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Diagonal Matrix
content.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{6}^{-1} & \,\,\,0 & 0 \\ \,\,0 & \,(-9)^{-1} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{18}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{8}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {4}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Diagonal Matrix
content.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{8}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {4}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{6}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Diagonal Matrix
content.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{6}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Singular Value Decomposition
content.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
